newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Advancing Zaire rebels take rail town in south.
newsitem.headline: Advancing Zaire rebels take rail town in south.

text.p: Rebels took Zaire's southern rail town Kamina on Monday, effectively cutting off the copperbelt province of Shaba and hundreds of troops there from the rest of the country, expatriate and other sources said.
Zairean troops ran off without a fight and traditional chiefs set out as a late-night welcoming committee to greet Laurent Kabila's forces, the sources added.
Traders and businessmen confirmed the fall of the town.
"The rebels arrived at about two in the morning," said one expatriate in Shaba's capital Lubumbashi, 600 km (400 miles) to the south east.

Shaba's pro-autonomy governor Kyungu wa Kumwanza, appointed only four days ago, said there had been fighting in Kamina but could not confirm it had fallen to the rebels. "As far as I know both sides have retired to their respective bases," he said.

The sources said that in a familiar pattern in Zaire's five-month-old civil war, Zairean troops had fled three hours before the rebels arrived in what used to be the army's main southern garrison town and air base.

Some 150 soldiers -- possibly the only ones who had still been defending Kamina -- commandeered trains to head south to Lubumbashi, according to the sources who had contact with Kamina until radio links and telephones went dead early Monday.
Expatriates speculated that with rolling stock in Kamina and diesel to power it, the rebels could give pursuit by train, speeding their advance, unless the line was blocked.
Rebels or sympathisers also reportedly control Kasenga, which is only 220 km (130 miles) northeast of Lubumbashi.
The sources said the rebels had approached Kamina from the northeast, following -- on foot -- a branch railway line from the inland port of Kalemie, in north Shaba, which they took in February.
Monday's news sent a shiver of apprehension round the Shaban capital of around one million people, Zaire's biggest city after the capital Kinshasa and potentially its richest.
Lubumbashi is still in government hands but its people say they are waiting for the rebels.
Much looted in past unrest, the city fears more of the same from soldiers based here or the retreating newcomers, some of whom were only hours away by rail.
There were no reports of major looting in Kamina, though some soldiers stole cars from a convent and roughed up a Belgian expatriate in the town.

Government forces in Shaba are now virtually cut off, their only escape routes a tortuous trek along the Angolan border, planes to Kinshasa 1,800 km (1,200 miles) away to the west, or escape to Zambia or Angola.

Traders and businessmen in Lubumbashi confirmed the fall of Kamina, which sits on the railway that is the sole reliable route to bring much-needed supplies up from southern Africa to the diamond-mining Kasai province and its capital Mbuji-Mayi.
Rebel leaders, seeking to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko, say they hope to start peace talks with the government later this week. In the meantime, they march on.
Kabila, from Shaba himself, now holds a quarter of the Central African country which is the size of Western Europe.
